Question: The probability that event \(A\) occurs is \(\frac34;\) the probability that event \(B\) occurs is \(\frac23.\) Let \(p\) be the probability that both \(A\) and \(B\) occur. The smallest interval necessarily containing \(p\) is the interval
Solution:
The event that both \(A\) and \(B\) occur is contained in \(B\), so
\[
p\le P(B)=\frac23.
\]
For the lower bound, adding \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\) counts their overlap twice. Subtracting it once gives
\[
P(A\cup B)=\frac34+\frac23-p
=\frac{17}{12}-p.
\]
A probability cannot exceed 1, so
\[
\frac{17}{12}-p\le1,
\qquad p\ge\frac5{12}.
\]

To show that this interval cannot be shortened, take any \(p\) between these bounds. Assign probabilities to the four possible occurrence patterns as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\text{both})&=p,\\
P(\text{only }A)&=\frac34-p,\\
P(\text{only }B)&=\frac23-p,\\
P(\text{neither})&=p-\frac5{12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Throughout the proposed interval, these four numbers are nonnegative and sum to 1. They give the required probabilities \(P(A)=3/4\) and \(P(B)=2/3\). Thus every value in the interval, including both endpoints, is possible. The smallest necessary interval is \(\boxed{[\frac5{12},\frac23]}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
